Photoacoustic tomography (PAT) represents a promising noninvasive medical imaging technique that combines high optical absorption contrast with the deep imaging capabilities and safety of ultrasonic detection. Public concern over hardware security has surged, prompting buyers to inspect specifications for elements like Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and secure enclaves. However, existing isolations rely heavily on complex, proprietary architectures that are untrusted by users and often expose side-channels. We propose Trust-Isle, a hardware enclave designed to minimize trust by using only components widely regarded as secure, omitting all other execution-environment-specific features. By relying on the simplicity, robustness, and accessibility of trusted primitives, Trust-Isle circumvents the typical execution and isolation complexities, thereby reducing the likelihood of side-channel vulnerabilities while remaining practical to trust. The system integrates trusted storage, trusted execution, trusted memory encryption, and trusted I/O into a cohesive system architecture. We validated the feasibility of Trust-Isle by porting and evaluating multiple real-world applications, comparing them against state-of-the-art platforms. The study demonstrates that despite its stripped-down design, Trust-Isle remains competitive in both performance and security.

Traditional reinforcement learning methods operate under the assumption of accessing i.i.d. samples from parametric generative models, a constraint that causes learning to stall when these models are inaccurate or corrupted. In contrast, this work investigates Reinforcement Learning with Imperfect Systems (PLI), which aims to learn an optimal policy using non-i.i.d. data that may contain strong corruption from a potentially hostile environment. The study applies this framework to multi-agent settings where a goal-oriented task requires coordinating with agents operating at lower levels of complexity. It demonstrates that standard multi-agent policy learning techniques fail when confronted with such heavy corruption, subsequently introducing Policy Learning with Imprecise Agents (PLI) as a specialized family of algorithms capable of building reliable generative representations from highly degraded data. Theoretical analysis establishes the sample and computational expense required for these methods to achieve an $\epsilon$-optimal policy, while empirical tests across standard and corrupted versions of StarCraft II validate the practical viability of the approach.

Lattice-scale electronic inhomogeneity is a prevalent feature across various magnetic high-Tc superconductors, though its origins remain debated, with theories ranging from external causes like cooling rate impurities to intrinsic many-body electronic effects. Addressing this discussion, we present angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) data from the natively occurance-ordered magnetic semiconductor CuFe2S3. Our findings reveal a 10 eV energy gap between orbitals, demonstrating that many-body interactions within the pyridine triplet (TP) system drive electrons to occupy specific orbitals.

This study examines the optical properties of a two-dimensional monolayer transition metal dichalcogenide under strong spin-orbital coupling conditions, specifically investigating the role of dark excitons as a function of exciton momentum. At low energy scales, the system exhibits a spontaneous breaking of rotational symmetry characterized by alternating high and low dark Rabi frequencies. Unlike similar phenomena in ferromagnetic materials, these fluctuations occur without the need for an external magnetic field. Furthermore, the optical behavior varies distinctly between monolayer and bilayer structures; while single layers allow fluctuations to impact both photoluminescence and absorption, such effects are suppressed in bilayer systems.

We introduce the concept of single-photon quantum optica; it involves designing nonlinear interactions where a single-photon component enables multi-photon functionality. Utilizing this framework, we investigate a specific model where a mode interacts with three others through an SPQC process (Single-Photon Quantum Catalysis). We demonstrate that generating one or more coherent multi-photon quanta within a single mode, contingent upon an input single-photon trigger, becomes possible. Furthermore, the theory distinguishes itself by allowing precise regulation of linear and quadratic couplings via magnetic flux and phase parameters. The model exhibits distinctive features, such as the creation of multi-photon Fock states in a mode without an external oscillatory drive, which is initiated simply by an input single photon. The associated phase in such superpositions can be tuned using the mode's particle number and the driving frequency. Additionally, the utilization of Tavis-Civil interactions allows the formation of hybrid states composed of a hybrid of single-photon and multi-photon coherent components within a mode, with controllable interference determined by the drive frequency relative to the couplings. The paper also discusses potential experimental realizations using circuit QED architectures, highlighting the generation of single-photon catalyzed coherent superpositions as a novel phenomenon.

In the latter case, when integrated into a Newman-Penrose formulation within General Relativity, these bivectors reveal that the Weyl tensor comprises only three distinct self-dual components, as opposed to the four found in the real-valued representation of the Riemann tensor. Subsequently, by re-expressing the Weyl tensor via complex, null tetrads in the gravitational analog of the Faraday formula, this method yields the standard Newman-Penrose variables. Furthermore, the paper identifies the geometric significance of the three invariants of the electromagnetic bivector when applied to the gravitational field. Specifically, it clarifies that these indices determine whether the spacetime is algebraically special of Weyl type N or type II, as well as whether it belongs to the radiative VSNS class.

This educational resource explores how dynamic optimization methods support enhanced patient care in Intensive Care Units, specifically focusing on dual-patient ventilation strategies developed during the COVID-19 pandemic. By enabling two patients to be ventilated simultaneously within a single bedside device, this technique allows clinicians to allocate the limited number of available machines to a greater number of patients, thereby increasing the capacity for patient care. Formulated as a Multiple Moving Interface Problem, the optimization model determines the most effective strategies for delivering appropriate tidal volumes and interface pressures across varying cycles to ensure safe ventilation. While numerical techniques for solving such multiple moving interface problems are discussed, this exploration highlights the practical development and application of such strategies with the specific context of dual-patient ventilation during the pandemic.

Delineating esophageal tumors in CT scans presents a dual challenge, stemming from the pathological spread of these cancers and the anatomical complexity of the thoracic region. While dense tumors often occupy multiple scans across the chest and abdominal areas, sparse tumors are confined within the difficult-to-differentiate thorax. Although standard segmentation typically relies on a global network architecture, the distinctiveness of these two tumor types suggests the advantage of specialized models. Furthermore, random sampling during training frequently results in an imbalance, where sparse tumors are underrepresented. Consequently, our proposed solution features two separate networks: Global Unet (GUnet) targets dense tumors, and Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet) specializes in sparse tumors. Addressing data scarcity, we implemented a training strategy that utilizes image replication and rotation to augment the limited number of available sparse scans. Additionally, the design of DDAUnet integrates several advanced modules, including dilated convolutions, dense connectivity blocks, a attention mechanism, to optimize its efficacy. Our framework was rigorously evaluated on a private dataset containing 77 scans from eight patients, utilizing metrics such as Dice coefficient, sensitivity, and specificity. During the drilling process, real-time adjustments are essential to optimize operational efficiency. However, accurately determining formation properties in real time presents significant challenges. Typically, formation evaluation relies on integrating data from well logs, which represent the historical physical properties of the formation. Although well logs are not always accessible in an offshore real-time context, they can be simulated using forward modeling tools that replicate how such logs are generated. These simulations yield predicted values and their associated uncertainties, which can then be compared against actual online sensor data to infer current formation properties and guide steering decisions. This paper introduces an uncertainty-quantified ensemble Kalman filter designed for forward geosteering integration. The approach combines a log simulation model with downhole pressure and temperature sensors to estimate formation characteristics in real time. The method's validity and performance are assessed using data from a horizontal well targeting a carbonate reservoir in the Gulf of Mexico.

Multilingual communities frequently utilize a blend of two or more languages within their communication. Although prior research predominantly focused on code-separated or inherently code-switched datasets, increasing real-world demand now drives interest in addressing code-switched Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. As these datasets are rapidly expanding, the following paper explores key aspects and potential obstacles associated with developing for code-switched languages, while also presenting positive findings and strategies to mitigate identified challenges in the field.

Automatic Image Description (AID) systems depend heavily on annotated reference data, both for training and evaluation. However, the application of these references for assessing generated descriptions often assumes an optimal quality that may not reflect reality. This study introduces a method to evaluate the utility of reference data for AID assessment by analyzing the interplay between exact matching with existing answers, semantic similarity to those answers, and human judgment. Results indicate that an increasing number of established features in image annotation tools yield a higher concentration of well-qualified responses during human reviews. Crucially, utilizing multiple qualified references for evaluation substantially enhances accuracy compared to using a single primary answer, even when those answers exhibit strong overall semantic qualities. These insights hold significant value for optimizing AID model development, particularly in contexts where computational resources are too limited to deploy extensive evaluation metrics during the training phase.

Tantalum oxides (Ta$_2$O$_5$) are renowned for their diverse phase transitions, which span from insulating to metallic and finally superconducting regimes. In this study, we identified a novel monoclinic crystal structure for the Ta2O5 glass ground state by evaluating its total energy within *ab-initio* simulations, a structure that matches the energy levels of structures currently observed experimentally. Molecular dynamics simulations, employing the Embedded Atom Method (EAM), were utilized to demonstrate that cooling liquid tantalum from the melt results in this specific structure at the glass transition temperature. These simulations indicate that the primary mechanism behind the formation of the glass is phase separation into metal-rich and metal-poor clusters, which become frozen as the system reaches the transition temperature upon cooling.

As Internet bandwidth expands, an increasing volume of malicious activities utilize high-speed channels to execute covert operations, execute massive tasks, or execute malicious actions while evading countermeasures designed to block them. A primary objective for active defense is identifying these activities; however, traditional detection mechanisms often rely on assuming malicious traffic uses concealed or unreliable channels, failing to recognize that adversaries now leverage legitimate, high-capacity networks to execute both overt and concealed attacks simultaneously. This paper introduces a novel statistical framework specifically for suspicious incident detection within normal, high-volume data streams. The proposed method addresses statistical dependencies in time-series packets using Copulas and identifies anomalies via change-point detection within their transformed standard normal equivalents. Validated through real-world experiments spanning web logs, file transfers, and DNS queries, the approach effectively identifies various malicious events, including distributed computing activities, copyright piracy, DNS spoofing, and volumetric DDoS attacks, achieving superior precision and recall with significantly quicker identification times than existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Human demonstration serves as a primary method for task learning, with demonstrators utilizing visual, auditory, and haptic cues to aid learning; yet, understanding of how human demonstrators utilize hand manipulations of end-effectors to convey intended actions remains limited. This study examines the auditory characteristics demonstrated by multiple individuals when signaling a desired robot manipulation. Results indicate that for both intended and physically executed movements, sound intensity patterns provide robust discrimination of intentions, with high intensity utilized to draw attention to specific non-executed movements. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a functional dependency between vibration frequency and spatial orientation of movements, suggesting such frequencies act as an implicit spatial indicator. Finally, the research explores the interplay between visual execution and actual movement initiation to clarify how human operators regulate auditory feedback during demonstration.

A **mixed-type tree** is defined as an infinite, locally finite, rooted tree where the subunits are finite. This paper introduces a straightforward algorithm designed to uniformly generate $n$-vertex subtrees (both type-matched and otherwise) drawn from the infinite tree described above. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through easily implemented Python code.

The Euler-Arnold equations, defined on a Euclidean space with a non-degenerate metric space structure, serve as a formal analogy to flow equations on groups. Within a Euclidean city space metric, these equations support a family of superposition. By applying this result within an urban space metric, we derive a conformal field theory; specifically, the spaces and city metric define a space with a large symmetry group. The group symmetry yields a large group of transformations, and the city space metric is invariant under a Wess-Zumino-Witten theory with Euclidean space defined as transformations. We show that Euclidean space with large symmetry city grid satisfies Euler-Arnold equations in dual form, indicating a duality between Euler-Arnold equations, large symmetry city grid, and Wess-Zumino-Witten theory with dual spaces.

Conversational Agents (CA) have become increasingly popular, serving as the interface for numerous mass-used applications. Although their user base expands, the reliability of these systems often lags behind, primarily because current testing methods are immature, making bugs difficult to detect early. Addressing this gap, we present an assessment of ten widely used CAs that reveals a prevalent and severe bug class we term "Involuntary Utterance (IVU)"—an issue where the agent speaks unintentionally, such as completing user sentences or initiating speech mid-conversation. Enabling our findings, we introduce AUTOTEST, a framework designed to automate the generation, execution, and evaluation of conversations. By integrating a customizable dialogue management engine, execution APIs for diverse CAs, and adaptable testing actions, it streamlines the validation process for various conversational applications. Beyond measuring the reliability of ten CAs, our system effectively identifies and rectifies significant bugs like IVU, thereby advancing the testing maturity of conversational agents.

Various theories suggest a massive, Earth-like planet (Planet X) orbits beyond Neptune, yet its discovery has proven elusive despite numerous searches. A primary hypothesis is that its gravitational influence could be detected as anomalous movements in known planets. To evaluate this, we simulated the gravitational effects of a 10 $M_{\oplus}$ Planet X across three scenarios: as an isolated body, within a system of nine known planets, and in the actual observed solar system. We employed a high-precision integrator (REBOUND) and a semi-empirical model of the inner solar system (REPOBS) to determine which planets would show measurable deviations. Our results indicate that regardless of the model, the most significant deviations occur in Venus and Jupiter. Specifically, if Planet X exists solely alone, deviations for both are minimal ($< 10$ m/day). However, in the real solar system context, deviations reach 20 m/day for Venus and 40 m/day for Venus and Jupiter, respectively. Consequently, the largest impacts are on inner-system planets like Venus, whereas outer planets show relatively minor effects. This asymmetry implies that Planet X would likely be identifiable through astrometric data from Venus, making this a viable detection strategy.

Translating text involves drawing upon extensive world knowledge, often resulting in difficulties that current neural machine translation models struggle to address effectively. Equipping machines with explicit knowledge is theoretically advantageous, yet existing approaches require parallel bilingual dictionaries and significant additional training data. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a new method for training machine translation systems using only monolingual dictionary memory. During the process of creating translation pairs, we define a special joint state that allows us to update the memory with words from the source language alone, thereby avoiding any need for target vocabulary updates or reliance on target side data. As these learned memories function somewhat as dynamic vocabulary dictionaries, initial translation performance remains lower because the system must balance known lexicon items against general distribution patterns. However, by fine-tuning the model on small amounts of training data, performance improves markedly compared to standard settings, surpassing base versions by up to 3.6 BLEOU on the M21 benchmark dev set. Furthermore, since the proposed technique does not utilize target dictionaries, it yields greater improvements in settings where lexicons are of poor quality, increasing performance by 1.2 BUOU on the same dev set.

Within Conformal Cyclic Cosmology, the transition between one universe and the very next occurs as the current expanding phase approaches an asymptotic limit of de Smann evolution. This future expansion is predicted to slow until our expansive universe attaches to a future "freeze" state. Contrarily, at the beginning of every subsequent universe, conditions resemble those we experience profoundly now. Therefore, if valid, remnants known as Hossels from the end of our universe would manifest as strange temperature irregularities called anomalies in the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB). This manuscript explores specific types of anomalies in the CMB and discusses how they might be interpreted as evidence of Hossels, including linear features called Hoose lines, circular spots known as Hoose circles, and fluctuations called Hoss fluctuations.

Few-shot learning is dedicated to categorizing new classes using minimal labeled examples, a capability that enables the expansion of data annotation domains beyond traditional methods. In this study, we address the task of few-shot learning as a meta-learning challenge. We introduce a new methodology that derives type-based prototypes to represent each category. This approach operates in an episodic framework where the model trains on a single task per session. By deriving prototypes directly from instance support sets, this method avoids reliance on external embeddings, allowing them to be learned specifically for each task. We validate the effectiveness of this prototype-based approach through extensive testing on the standard mini-ImageNet and few-ImageNet benchmarks. Additionally, we incorporate a contrastive learning strategy to refine the prototypes' discriminative power. Our experimental results indicate that these contrastively enhanced prototypes achieve state-of-the-art performance on both mini-ImageNet and few-ImageNet datasets.

Recommendation systems for music have evolved across multiple phases, initially relying on content analysis, then moving to user feedback, and subsequently driving listening behaviors. Existing approaches addressing the sparsity problem in these contexts can be categorized into implicit-content methods (using metadata) and community-driven models (leveraging similar artists). However, these traditional techniques often falter when recommending for users with sparse profiles. To bridge this gap, we propose a Cooperative Content-and-Community-Based (C4) framework tailored to such sparse sparse-scenarios. This model integrates the Music Genome content profiles with Last.fm’s music similarity graphs. A notable limitation of current C4 methods is their failure to capture the nuanced, multi-dimensional preferences inherent in complex content profiles; as a result, we introduce a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MS-DCR) algorithm. The core of our solution is an Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (ECAPL) module designed to synthesize latent content and community preferences robustly. Our extensive experiments on a public dataset confirm the superior efficacy of the proposed approach.

This extension of the Hypatia package for Julia focuses on methods for solving natural conic equations. It encompasses the resolution of homogeneous and affine equations within both elliptic and hyperbolic spaces, as well as the determination of solutions on the real projective space through the solving of arbitrary projective conic equations. Given that Natural Geometry serves as a subset of Natural Linear Algebra—which manages algebraic operations constrained to the boundaries of vector spaces—this new functionality inherently necessitates the implementation of various natural transformations, such as the diction between skew-symmetric matrices and conics, or the mapping between matrices of ordinal parameters and lines.

Automated systems for assessing MRI quality are now widely used in clinical environments to ensure these images meet the necessary standards before analysis. Deep learning models have demonstrated effectiveness in predicting scores based on MRI artifacts; however, these models struggle when deployed with data drawn from diverse settings, such as different data centers, MRI scanners, or when compared against hand-crafted evaluations by experts. To address these issues, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of multiple convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures. Our findings indicate that solving this problem requires separating the task into two distinct components: first, learning the characteristics of those artifacts, and second, learning the assessment criteria themselves. We support this hypothesis with a generalization analysis of six different CNNs. Furthermore, we developed a new dual-branch architecture that successfully validates the approach by surpassing previous single-branch methods in both hand-crafted and simulated environments.

This paper offers comprehensive performance evaluations of the Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory module (model 6800), which functions as a memory expansion to DDR4 and is priced comparably to traditional Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM). While vendors often highlight its throughputs based on NAND-like interface metrics, this study reveals significantly greater nuance in memory system behavior through extensive analysis of both synthetic and application-driven workloads. Our experiments explore various levels of Optane caching strategies within the DDR4 environment, leveraging profiling tools to dissect CPU and memory system interactions. By examining optimizing techniques for specific applications, our results establish a robust performance baseline that effectively guides future architectural investigations. Ultimately, this research provides practical insights for integrating Optane modules, demonstrating significant potential for enhancing database operations when paired with appropriate I/O interfaces, such as the Optane DC Persistent Memory Direct Access (DMA) interface. Consequently, these measurements serve as a foundational reference, illustrating how Optane modules can improve overall application efficiency by deepening our understanding of the integrated system.

Motivated by the need to lower meeting costs for distributed teams, this paper explores a new approach to scheduling multi-agent recurrent meetings. We introduce the Drive-Based Motivation (DBM) algorithm, which models a motivated agent using a drive parameter. This parameter integrates an agent's intrinsic factors—such as age, agent type, and connectivity—along with extrinsic inputs like regularity coefficients and Albrecht coefficients (derived from message counts). This model supports various meeting topologies, ranging from star and line structures to fully connected networks, and our methods are validated through simulations.

This study presents outcomes from a first-principles investigation into the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds. Using the Full-Potential Linearized Augmented Plane Wave (FP-LAPW) method within the Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA) framework, researchers analyzed the pure compounds GdSn$_3$ and CmSn$_3$ alongside their alloyed counterparts, Gd$_{0.25}$Cm$_{0.75}$Sn$_3$ and Gd$_{0.5}$Cm$_{0.5}$Sn$_3$. It was determined that both individual compounds are stable under the P6$_3$/mmc space group. Furthermore, applying the coherent potential approximation (CPA) method allowed for an exploration of the alloyed compounds' characteristics. According to the findings, both GdSn$_{0.25}$Cm$_{0.75}$Sn$_{0.5}$ and GdSn$_{0.25}$Cm$_{0.75}$Sn$_{0.5}$ exhibit lower total energy and enhanced mechanical resilience. Additionally, the materials' magnetic responses were analyzed by inducing magnetic moments on non-target compounds. Finally, the study concludes that the alloyed compounds display improved stability, making them promising candidates for magnetic applications.

The methodology involves applying the well-validated phenomenological coalescence model to analyze particle formation during hadronization. Based on simulations of central Pb+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV, we observe that significant yields of these particles arise from mechanisms beyond standard coalescence. Specifically, our model forecasts substantial production of $\Lambda_c$ baryons, $D$ mesons, and various quarkonia states such as $J/\Psi$ and $\Upsilon$. These measurements were obtained using data from the CMS detector at the LHC.

This paper establishes a generalization of the foundation theorem applicable to B-type finite Coxeter groups. It introduces the B-type combinatorial Matriux complex and demonstrates that the B-type finite Coxeter group acts as a matrix group upon the B-type combinatorial matrix complex, effectively generalizing the existing theorem of E. S. Vassiliev regarding the finite type A (C(n,1)) matrix group. The proof strategy involves the inductive determination of a specific set of generators and their corresponding relations.

Weak gravitational lensing induces slight variations in the observed brightness of distant objects due to foreground mass inhomogeneities; while this effect complicates precision cosmology by influencing distance measurements, it can also be harnessed as an observational tool. By compiling weak lensing shear measurements for nearby Type Ia supernovae from the Pantheon dataset, we handle this phenomenon as both a challenge and an opportunity. Utilizing a dataset of 42 nearby Pantheon events with 1.8–2.3 redshifts, we calculated the input and output shear matrices by integrating a generalized version of the efficient P2GPU ray-tracing algorithm, processing over one hundred million particles. Our refined methodology yields a robust 8×8 matrix for each individual supernova, enabling precise point mass estimations and the first-ever determination of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) utilizing only shear data ($H_0^{shear} = 69.6^{+4.4}_{-4.5}$). When combined with luminosity distance and sample mean constraints from Pantheon ($H_0^{combined} = 70.1 \pm 3.0$), this result offers a consistent and complementary assessment. Furthermore, utilizing luminosity distance information allows for $1\sigma$ detections of substructure within individual halos, achieving a mean recovery accuracy of approximately 14%.

This investigation offers a detailed comparison of the efficacy of line selection schemes, specifically exploring both parametric and randomised methods, within the framework of least-squares deconvolution (LSD). The assessment focuses on mitigating stellar variability, measured by full width at half-maximum (FIM) velocity precision, across various activity-driven noise models, including Gaussian and spotted surface variations. The parametric approach demonstrates its customary strength against Gaussian noise; however, the randomised strategy proves superior in scenarios involving noise generated by spots, consistently yielding better performance than the parametric model. Advancing this versatility, the implementation of activity correction prior to the randomised deployment significantly enhances velocity accuracy, particularly on stars exhibiting spotted surfaces, achieving up to a factor of two improvement in certain cases.

Autonomous data collection in wireless sensor networks faces two primary hurdles: estimating link transmission qualities, which varies due to changes in quality of service and query demand, and collection tree construction, a process complicated by the network's flat architecture and dynamic nature. To address these issues, we propose a two-phase collection tree algorithm. In the first phase, a range-based method utilizes bidirectional link quality estimation to partition the network into hierarchical clusters. The second phase organizes these clusters into a dedicated collection tree. This link quality approach decouples tree construction from the specific services requirements, while the resulting hierarchical structure enables an efficient, tree-like architecture. Collectively, this method mitigates energy bottlenecks by significantly reducing control overhead and duplicate transmissions. Numerical simulations confirm the algorithm's efficacy, demonstrating rapid convergence, lower collection latency, and reduced energy consumption.

How does your detection performance vary across different real-world contexts? We introduce a straightforward and practical framework to help answer this question, enabling evaluators to identify the distribution of several intrinsic and user-defined characteristics within their operational environments. Using deep-based object detectors as a use case, we demonstrate that providing labeled data pertaining to these features allows models to leverage them for augmentation or adaptation. Ultimately, we show that benchmarking against a diverse set of contexts is essential for ensuring robust deployment in new settings. All visualizations and interactive tools necessary to implement this framework in practice are available as part of this paper's code release at https://github.com/lcshen/pr_context.

When a kidney becomes available from the deceased donor pool, we determine the best strategy for an living donor patient by evaluating their eligibility for a hospital-approved optimal unmatched-organ matching algorithm. Using a stochastic dynamic programming framework, we establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for the optimality of an $(n+1)$-matched donor matching policy, where $n$ is the current number of kidneys already owned. We evaluate numerical simulations across varying parameter sets to analyze how matching thresholds shift in response to specific economic, medical, and ethical considerations.

Implicit user preference models are essential for achieving personalized information retrieval, a task that explicit data often cannot fully support due to sparsity. These models infer preferences from behavior, which includes interactions like item clicks, dwell time, concurrent items, and post-purchase actions. Implicit Ties, authored by Elizabeth M. Kim and colleagues, summarizes these methods with an emphasis on their application to information seeking, though much of this content is transferable to other domains. The piece begins by outlining the theory behind implicit preference generation and describes data types, such as logs, that capture user interactions. It then reviews modeling strategies divided into matrix factorization approaches, which infer preferences from direct interactions, and relevance models, which derive preferences by analyzing the sequence logic of observed behaviors. The article concludes with an examination of evaluation metrics, testing methodologies, and identified research opportunities within implicit modeling. This overview serves both those seeking to build new factorization models and those aiming to integrate them with relevance-based approaches, which is often necessary given that observed actions rarely reflect singular, isolated preferences.

While word2vec and similar embedding techniques remain popular for financial text analysis, unassessed usage poses risks. This study first challenges whether pre-trained models capture semantic relations among corporate report sections, using an assessment protocol that reveals embedded finance terms often cluster poorly. Furthermore, we investigate the justification for utilizing pre-trained embeddings when segmenting 10-K documents with the Loughran-McDonald (LM) dictionary, offering a practical framework to validate document-scoping decisions. Our analysis indicates that training-from-scratch approaches yield superior or comparable classification for most 10-K sections, except those containing legal text, suggesting that "out-of-the-box" embeddings are not universally preferable. Finally, we address "finetuning" decisions, demonstrating that initializing with BERT and GLoVe produces results inferior to standard setups.

"This study introduces a novel approach that integrates the level-set method with a built-in boundary technique to efficiently manage moving interfaces within two-phase flow simulations. While preserving the storage efficiency of embedded boundaries near movement interfaces, our proposal addresses their primary drawback—difficulty in handling topological alterations—by leveraging level-sets for this specific function. Employing a Cartesian grid, we formulate the hybrid strategy to simulate a heating element's movement within a melting container, using it as a benchmark. Using a cooling source instead, we utilize the model as a test case for verifying storage modifications and implement various grid resolutions to investigate numerical dissipation. The results from the simulation demonstrate the method's capacity to capture thin interfaces with minimal numerical smearing, supporting conclusions drawn from previous research into embedded boundary/immersed methods regarding low dissipation. The method is accurate and efficient, making it suitable for simulating complex interfaces with complicated changes in shape."

Current interpretations of linguistics utilize a non-commutative variant of type theory, often referred to as the calculus of endogenous functions. Within this syntactic framework, we introduce a spin term by integrating the linear calculus with quantum mechanics. Our approach reinterprets the role of unary operators, offering a quantum analysis that complements the classical calculus. Specifically, we examine the quantifier and modal operators found in natural language, exploring how their compositionality emerges through interaction with other linguistic operators.

Current methods for training game agents in competitive settings typically rely on approximating equilibrium strategies; however, their methodical steps often produce non-intelligible explanations, creating hurdles for both professional competitors and regular users. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for End-to-end (e2e) learning of human-comprehensible tree-based neural network (TTN) representations of equilibria in multiplayer games. Our contributions include a new algorithm, ExpTreeNet, which computes such explainable structures. We applied ExpTreeNet to two-player zero-sum scenarios (specifically in Extensive-Form Games or EFGs) and general-sum multiplayer games (in Normal-Form Games or NFGs). Our findings indicate that ExpTreeNet successfully generates neural strategy policies paired with robust, intuitive, and consistent global justifications that outperform existing approaches in clarity. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of these explainable trees as a foundation for AI teammates in multiplayer contexts. Our methods hold the potential to advance the development of more transparent, trustworthy, and effective competitive game AIs.

This study examines the spread of epidemics on networks that incorporate preventive rewiring, occurring as individuals exceed a specific infection probability threshold to replace some connections at random with new ones. Using the Susceptible-Infected (SI) framework, we fit the exact network topology dynamics with mean-field equations to efficiently trace network evolution. By applying the boundaries of the SI network as constraints, we derive an associated Hamiltonian and utilize the variational approach to determine its most probable steady state. Within this model, a basic epidemic curve emerges when the basic reproduction number surpasses unity, with the network reaching a unique endemic equilibrium; furthermore, the article investigates the topology's impact on peak infection levels and final outbreak sizes within the network structure.

Nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds constitute a significant class of almost contact metric manifolds that encompasses a wide variety of examples. In this study, we examine the Cotton tensor field on almost contact metric manifolds and determine its divergence. As an application, we identify the conditions required for the existence of Cotton soliton on nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds, specifically proving that such structures are trivial and the scalar of any Cotton soliton equals $-3$.

This study presents a theoretical framework within the Standard Model designed to support modern global fits of the proton parton distribution functions (PDFs). Addressing both theoretical and phenomenological elements, this model accounts for parton evolution, quark-hadron duality, hadronization, and the transition between perturbative and non-perturbative regimes. These features are mathematically expressed to align with the current computational strategies used in state-of-the-art PDF fitting suites. Lastly, this model serves as a foundational basis for proposed future fits incorporating hadron PDFs and a dynamic interface between perturbative and non-perturbative physics.

In the domain of reinforcement learning, Experience Replay serves as a fundamental technique that enhances sample efficiency and stabilizes training by recycling past experiences. Nevertheless, standard Experience Replay treats all stored data with uniform sampling probability, ignoring the statistical variability of states and actions. This lack of discrimination leads to an imbalanced state where certain trajectories are overrepresented while others are underutilized, particularly concerning the inherent stochasticity of the policy optimization process itself.

Consequently, this study introduces Variance Diminution based Experience Replay (VDR). The core objective of VDR is to mitigate training imbalance through the introduction of a variance-reduced importance weight. Achieved via the application of Control Variates, variance reduction ensures more precise, low-fluctuation estimates of these importance weights. Furthermore, to guarantee a uniform distribution during the reinforcement learning process, the algorithm incorporates multiple reservoirs, each maintaining distinct representative statistics of actions and states. Empirical results across various tasks demonstrate that the proposed method significantly surpasses the performance of current leading state-of-the-art approaches.

Similarly, identifying the authentic gap structure in these materials is difficult, largely because standard light elements like potassium induce significant lattice distortions upon replacing barium, leading to intense interference between electron holes and electron pockets. Consequently, determining the gap on the dominant heavy pockets has proven nearly impossible. Addressing this in $(\text{Ba}_{0.6}\text{K}_{0.4})\text{Fe}_2\text{As}_2$, we employed highly doped samples (approximately 98% level) combined with $K$-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) measurements of the unoccupied $p$-orbitals in potassium to precisely track interference patterns and eliminate its confounding effects. Furthermore, by utilizing the first-principles augmented plasma approach (FAP) within angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) frameworks, we achieved clarity on the interference issue. Our analysis confirms that the low-energy $d$-like bands observed in ARPES actually originate from many-body corrections, while the true underlying band structure is of character. Finally, gap analysis reveals a $s_{\pm}$ superconducting state characterized by a nodal structure.

Recently, a generalized version of the hubbard-Stratonovich transformation was formulated within the framework of the theory of stochastic processes. Applying this theory to various models of phase transitions, it enables the reconstruction of critical exponents in systems exhibiting second-order transitions, even in instances where standard methods fail due to the presence of imaginary critical modes in the effective action. In this study, we compare this novel method against the super-variationization equation, a component of modern bosonization theory capable of handling imaginary modes. Utilizing ${}^{8}$Li $\beta$-detected NMR to probe the electronic characteristics of LaNiO$_3$ is a recent innovation. We employed this technique to examine the evolution of a LaNiO$_3$-based metallic phase within LaAlO$_3$ superlattices. By examining varying numbers of NiO$_3$ monolayers, we investigated how electronic structure develops. Our findings reveal a rapid build-up of magnetic moments during early stages of growth, where a clear metallic phase emerges even at a thickness of just three monolayers. Furthermore, increasing the NiO$_3$ layer count enhances both magnetic moments and moments of inertia, with these properties converging towards those of a bulk LaNiO$_3$ film. The observed behavior aligns well with theoretical predictions.

We introduce MultiTalk, a dialogue testbed designed to explore diverse and varied conversations. Although current dialogue models have achieved remarkable progress, their evaluation heavily relies on two publicly available datasets featuring highly structured and linear interactions. This over-dependency on simplified scenarios has likely constrained the full assessment of dialogue systems' true capabilities. As a potential solution, we established MultiTalk by integrating a diverse collection of existing datasets, creating a dense network of dialogues characterized by superior variety in topic shifts and conversational depths. Our analysis, which incorporates topic dynamics, linguistic diversity, and a range-based evaluation of dialogue states across multiple levels, confirms that MultiTalk effectively captures heterogeneous interactions. Furthermore, as a continuous framework established through dataset synthesis, this structure allows for the scalable addition of new data sources. Finally, we observe a general decline in the confidence of state-of-the-art evaluators when scoring dialogues within this complex multi-branch environment, suggesting a clear necessity for more sophisticated evaluation metrics.

Integrating intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) into wireless networks offers a promising pathway to overcome spectrum scarcity and enhance data rates. This study analyzes the long-term throughput of a one-way wireless link comprising a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) transmission, an IRS with passive elements, and a single-antenna receiver. To model the correlation between phase-shift configurations and signal reflections more accurately, we propose a correlated Rician model. Furthermore, we derive the exact cumulative distribution function (CDF) and probability density function (PDF) for the received signal's instantaneous power by accounting for large-scale fading, correlation among phase-shifts, and practical, hardware-limited models for these shifts. Building on these statistical characterizations and assuming ergodic fading channels, we establish closed-form expressions for the system's long-term (ergodic) throughput. In addition, to understand behavior under large network deployments, we develop loose but analytically tractable lower bounds for the ergodic throughput. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations.

We analyze linear non-adiabatic stellar oscillations within a simplified one-dimensional model, consisting of an inert uniform core surrounded by a dynamical envelope where both gravity and opacity follow power-law variations. The model yields analytical analytical expressions for oscillation frequencies, revealing that certain regimes permit a mathematical separation of these frequencies into components: an inertial frequency determined by the core and a Lamb frequency characterizing the envelope. We term the regimes enabling such separation "topological regimes," and within them, we classify modes by counting the topological linkages between the Brunt-V\"ais\"al\"enel frequency and the separating power-law barriers in frequency and radial domains. This classification successfully identifies known modes in both the Sun and oscillation models. Furthermore, we demonstrate through perturbation analysis, accounting for modest deviations from power laws and non-ideal behavior, that these modes exhibit frequency shifts analogous to those in topological insulators. Specifically, perturbation induces mixing into non-topological components, thereby modifying their frequencies. Consequently, in topological stellar configurations, modes behave as bound states.

"The study of chimera states represents a vital avenue for understanding the collective behaviors in time-periodic systems, particularly within neural networks where groups of oscillators split into partial synchronization and other states that span a continuum. While recent work has shown a robustness against structural faults using homogeneous units, there is a lack of research on how heterogeneity influences these states. This paper presents findings on the sensitivity of traveling chimera states and linked patterns of synchronous clusters to parametric differences. We introduce a straightforward methodology based on the Fourier transform applied to spatial modes, enabling the easy identification of robust states. Most importantly, we propose a novel universal framework grounded in analysis based on frequency decomposition through this transformation, enabling identification of various patterns of occurrence in network dynamics, supplemented by measures of local coherence derived from modulation depth comparisons. We illustrate the application of this framework by simulating a simple Hopfield model under various conditions of heterogeneity, ultimately deriving analytical formulas to characterize the identified states. These formulas serve as the basis for designing new universal criteria, enabling classification into distinct categories such as robustness, anti-robustness, and ambiguous regions, and help distinguish between different types of global states. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to more complex networks composed of oscillators with different dynamics, and we suggest that it may serve as a valuable tool for analyzing experimental data.

Two-dimensional lattice gases are known for their rich and complex behavior, which is often influenced by the specific form of the interaction between sites. This study investigates a model on the square lattice incorporating nearest-neighbor repulsion in the complex-z plane (equivalent to the replica method) and analyzes high-temperature behavior using series expansions. The investigation focuses on how various ranges of nearest-neighbor interactions affect the system. Findings indicate a transition characterized by cluster formation, shifting from slow, linear growth of clusters under weak interactions to linear-$q$ growth in stronger interaction regimes, suggesting a transition between universality classes. The work also explores the impact of next-nearest-neighbor interactions and explores extensions of the model into higher dimensions.

If ultralight dark matter exists, its ubiquitous presence would enable neutrinos to undergo oscillations converting active neutrinos into sterile counterparts. In scenarios where active-sterile mixing occurs, even a sub-dense dark matter environment could dominate the universe's energy budget post-neutronization via such transformation. Consequently, this newly formed cosmological sea of neutrinos significantly alters the evolution of the early universe, including the duration of the cosmological transition, the scale of the initial collapse, the spectrum of primordial black holes, and the quantity of cosmic dark radiation. Furthermore, when considering $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay operations, the coherence of dark matter-induced neutrino oscillations can either enhance or diminish experimental constraints on this phenomenon compared to non-degenerate isolated sources, resulting in adjustment factors ranging up to $10^4$. Ultimately, the combined impacts of cosmological evolution and nuclear double-beta decay offer synergistic insights into the nature, density, and spatial distribution of dark matter.

The lack of detected ultra-high energy (UHE) photons, coupled with observations suggesting their rapid attenuation in the intergalactic pulsar magnetic fields, presents a mystery. While current models attribute this suppression to photon conversion into electron-positron pairs via interactions with light photons or the electromagnetic component of solar magnetic fields, there is a scarcity of quantitative calculations regarding the specific role of solar magnetic field-induced photon conversion. This study presents such calculations, focusing on pair production by UHE photons and solar light photons. The results indicate that for cosmic ray energies below 100 EeV, pairing with solar light photons dominates over other mechanisms, significantly reducing the flux of isotropic ultra-high energy photons. Consequently, the contribution from distant sources is most pronounced in the 10–100 EeV range. In contrast, for energies exceeding 100 EeV, photon propagation remains largely isotropic, as the flux is dominated by sources within our own galaxy. It is important to note that this conclusion assumes the solar magnetic field extends across most of the heliosphere; however, the primary limitation on UHE photon flux occurs well within this region, meaning the precise boundary of the field has limited relevance to the outcome.

Nonlocal theories of elasticity have evolved significantly over the past half-century, yet their application to gravity remains largely unexplored. This study introduces a nonlocal variant of the First Order Formalism within General Relativity, treating spacetime as possessing internal structure. The foundational mathematical tools of fundamental frames and relations are adapted for this purpose, and specific local and nonlocal constitutive frameworks are defined. Within these nonlocal models, stress becomes intrinsic, allowing us investigate stress-dependent spacetime geometries. The framework readily accommodates partial or incomplete gravity theories, yielding models of local and semi-local nonlocal gravity. Furthermore, the paper examines various fundamental and frame representations, clarifying the mathematical ties between nonlocal fundamental forms and local metric forms. A key finding demonstrates that fundamental frames are mathematically necessary within fundamental forms to ensure the theories remain nonlocal. By the end, it is asserted that both nonlocal versions of the First Order Formalism are mathematically viable and capable of producing rich, complex solutions.

Distributed systems utilize data replication to enhance availability and performance, often implementing replicate data as centralized servers with multiple copies to mitigate single points of failure. Due to the non-trivial latency of network communication, optimizations typically prioritize rapid data access over strict linear consistency, adopting approximations instead. Consequently, many systems adopt Change-crs (CRS-based) architectures, which are proven to be a viable foundation for constructing change-consistent, conflict-free replicated data structures (CRUD). However, these models do not support write operations, as concurrent writes from different locations create unresolvable conflicts. To fill this gap, we present Remove-Win, a universal framework for building conflict-free replicated data structures by integrating write operations with change-crs. We demonstrate the practicality of this approach by implementing two representative removal-based RDBs based on the framework. Our experiments indicate that RDB constructed via Remove-Win achieves roughly 40% more writes per second and 20% more reads per second, alongside 23% fewer pending operations compared to existing change-crs CRU systems.

The Wide Binary Test serves as the most accessible observational method for constraining light scalar fields, such as those predicted by Monodromy AdS/CFT-based string theories and alternative models like FIMPE. Widening the separation of wide binary star systems enhances the sensitivity of these bounds; however, wide binaries are also the most dynamically susceptible group, leading to complex orbital behaviors. The physical nature of the radio sources in our galaxy remains uncertain, with current models struggling to adequately explain both compact radio sources and the stochastic radio emission observed in our city's halo. To investigate these phenomena, we utilized large-scale, sensitive radio maps covering the Galactic plane to measure the spectral characteristics of the radio sources in our city using stacking. By processing updated sensitivity maps of the Galactic plane, we computed spectral indices for the radio sources in our city while preserving position information, thereby improving upon previous studies that integrated data across the entire Galactic plane. Our analysis reveals that when applied to sensitivity maps where data orientation information is retained, the resulting stacked data exhibits a spectral index approximately 0.5 less negative than when applying the method to the entire integrated galaxy plane. Furthermore, we performed a reanalysis of the previous study's data, confirming that the radio sources in our city show no preference for magnetic polar regions but are instead concentrated in areas active in our city.

This study analyzes fluid dynamics simulations of shocks propagating through a non-stirred medium under two conditions: those influenced by stellar winds and those occurring in vacuum. The winds result in distinct shock features, most notably envelope heating, while the primary driver for this heating mechanism is the rapid rise in shock velocity. In both scenarios, the shocks advance at super-Eddington velocities until they trigger a blowout event. However, the development of magnetic structures and the formation of reverse shocks are accelerated by the ambient medium, particularly in winds. Of substantial interest is the emergence of blastwaves within the outflow; these form when the primary shock transitions to a uniform, linear propagation speed. While the masses of reverse-shocked material and the peak velocities of the blastwave are larger in vacuum environments compared to stellar winds, both setups generate comparable masses of post-shocked gas following the onset of the blastwave phase.

We introduce an Natural Language Inference (NLI) task designed to identify diverse semantic interpretations within dialogues. In this framework, we provide three utterances for each example: a first statement, and a second statement that either contradicts or follows from the first, with the goal of determining which combination pairs with a third utterace that could serve as a plausible response. We argue that modeling how humans generate multiple potential next turns is essential for understanding and generating coherent conversation, and that leveraging NLI offers a cost-effective method to collect large-scale training datasets in this area. Our analysis reveals that using these dialogue diversity datasets significantly boosts the capability of open-book NLI models to distinguish between contradictory statements and those that are entailed by one another. Furthermore, we observe that top-tier natural language generation systems produce more varied and heterogeneous continuations when trained on this data, suggesting that such training helps mitigate the tendency of models to converge on predictable outputs. The study addresses Incremental Learning (IL), a framework where models are trained sequentially on a stream of concept-related tasks characterized by a skewed class distribution. To maintain performance in such imbalanced iterative environments, this research evaluates various methods for both measuring and correcting distributional biases. The paper explores multiple bias metrics, specifically focal loss, as well as convolutional neural network (CNN) enhancement strategies, including heterogeneous multi-scale (HMS) and homogeneous multi-scale (HMS) CNN architectures, along as memory integration. Although these techniques have been extensively utilized in standard IL literature, their efficacy remains questionable given the compounded difficulty of learning across several concepts under conditions of class imbalance. Consequently, this paper institutes a rigorous evaluative model for integrating various bias measurement and mitigation algorithms within an IL context, aiming to determine their relative effectiveness for skewed incremental scenarios.

Addressing the efficiency-frequency trade-off is vital in VLSI design, where techniques like voltage scaling and frequency retarding lower power consumption. Among available approaches, HyperDegrade introduces a novel method utilizing interconnect degradation to slow down a silicon chip. By applying HyperDegrade, researchers can transform a standard CPU from operating at 3.45 GHz to approximately 500 MHz, alongside other metrics such as an 11-fold increase in total latency, a 50-fold decrease in peak memory bandwidth, 100-fold decrease in peak arithmetic bandwidth, 3.45x decrease in L3 cache bandwidth, and 2.04 decrease in L2 cache bandwidth. Although the chip operates significantly slower, it maintains 85% of the original performance, with the remaining 15% loss in efficiency. Beyond these specific metrics, the paper provides a comprehensive study of this technique, detailing its application to various chips, the influence of different degradation strategies, and the underlying physical phenomena. By examining the impact on micro-architectures, HyperDegrade emerges as a promising avenue for enhancing the next generation of VLSI chips.

A multi-agent system capable of generating regular, grid-like patterns is described, where each agent measures its relative distances to adjacent agents in four orthogonal directions (north, south, east, and west). It is further determined that three specific constraints are necessary for stable relative equilibria: the directed interaction graphs for north-south and east-west links must possess tree structures with an odd number of nodes, the out-degrees in these graphs are constrained, and the overall topological complexity remains limited. Field-theoretic precision is now reaching a level of refinement that demands the resummation of large logarithms at every order. Within the region closely surrounding a radiation zero in irreducible rational kernels, these logs emerge from the interplay between reducible and irreducible kernels. Previously, we identified their tree-level structure and implemented an amplitude-based factorization scheme to manage them. Here, we extend this approach to higher orders by determining the leading logs within one-loop threshold residues. We establish their general form by identifying how one-loop rational kernels drive the branch-cut singularities present in one-loop threshold residues. Furthermore, we apply the method to QCD scattering amplitudes at two loops and the level of maximal helicity. While we successfully predict most logs using knowledge of the corresponding kernels for lower helicities, a discrepancy arises for two-plus helicities. In this specific case, the logs depend on two new constants: the one-loop irreducible kernel for two squares and the one-loop irreducible kernel for two plus helicities. Since the latter term lacks direct access, we suggest an alternative strategy for determining these logs.

Music festivals are renowned for their intense social interactions, creating significant opportunities for the rapid transmission of infectious diseases. While the existing literature highlights the general increase in social contact at these events, it overlooks the specific nature of that socializing. Our research investigates whether the nature of social interaction at festivals can facilitate the silent dissemination of malevolent behaviors disguised as positive ones. Drawing a parallel between social socializing at festivals and the algorithmic promotion of music streaming services, we propose that both environments foster 'virality.' In streaming contexts, user popularity data drives algorithms to recommend content based on the principle that if many listen, one likely should too. Similarly, the dense, impromptu social networks formed at festivals encourage rapid information exchange. We posited that if these systems foster viral adoption, they might also facilitate the widespread propagation of harmful acts if performed initially by just a few individuals. To examine this, we utilized data from a major U.S. festival and the streaming platform Spotify. Analysis of the festival data supported the hypothesis of dense social networking, while streaming analysis indicated a strong correlation between the number of existing adopters and the likelihood of new user adoption for any given song. These collective findings suggest a dangerous implication: because festivals and streaming algorithms both reward and facilitate viral adoption, they may serve as effective conduits for spreading detrimental patterns of conduct if such behaviors are enacted initially by only a small minority.

Participants in peer-to-peer storage markets face the challenge of determining how much to store based on prevailing market rates. Specifically, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for risk-averse equilibrium strategies, providing explicit risk functions that are quasi-concave in price. These mathematical characterizations serve as a foundational step for developing more complex, behavior-focused risk models in subsequent research.

Furthermore, it can be made coherent by integrating it into a multi-spike ensemble defined by periodic lattice structures. By leveraging the inherent characteristics of the lattice, the method yields a multi-bi-directional (MBD) state that is self-regulated and resistant to external perturbations. Comparisons indicate this theoretical approach surpasses current technological boundaries, holding promise for materially and surface-specific applications ranging from surface plasmons to catalytic processes. These applications could support novel functionalities such as manipulating charge transport or magnetism on ultrafast timescales.

Proposed as a backup to the Future Circular Collider, the e+e− circular electron-positron accelerator described here aims to operate at center-of-mass energies of 330 to 350 GeV. Comprising two primary stages—the Energy Upgrade (EU), which achieves 250 GeV and serves as the LHC's possible successor, and the Circe Collider (CC), designed for its high-energy run—this proposal outlines the "MU+/-/-" facility using circular paths for both low-and high-energy operations. Reaching a peak circle-of-mass energy of 100 GeV, it promises unprecedented luminosity for precision measurements, particle physics discoveries, and novel methodologies.

Respiration-related artifacts and signal inhomogeneity frequently compromise conventional free-breathing T2-weighted MRI. While existing motion-correction techniques for this sequence are limited, we propose an advanced turbo spin-echo (TSE) method that achieves rapid, respiration-gated imaging by synchronizing with the breathing cycle (3D+respiration dimensions) using a single, free-breathing acquisition. Our approach employs a newly developed motion-probability projection (MPP)—calculated from all k-space data analogous to standard respiratory bins—to derive real-time retrospective correction. Additionally, we implemented algorithmic steps to retroactively estimate the respiratory phase and apply offline gradient table modifications to retrospectively apply the necessary phase correction to each slice's z-gradient table. Validation on a phantom and in vivo studies (n=5 patients) demonstrated that these free-breathing, motion-compensated protocols yielded high image quality with no artifacts, matching turbo T2 images obtained under apnea across all anatomical regions. Specifically, compared to four-chute (4D) images reconstructed from free-breathing data, there were no significant differences in contrast, blur, or structural similarity indices (SSIM). Crucially, this technique significantly reduces scan duration: for equivalent or superior image quality, it is approximately four times faster than traditional 4D free-breathing methods.

This paper addresses secure control synthesis for unknown non-linear systems featuring input constraints and safety-critical operating regions. By leveraging input-dependent control barrier functions, the research proposes a model predictive control strategy that ensures constraint compliance while minimizing a given cost function. The proposed approach online solves a quadratic programming problem, making it computationally efficient. Additionally, the function used allows model complexity to remain lower, as it relies on per-structure representations rather than explicit system dynamics. The algorithm's performance and practical applicability were validated through simulation, utilizing an autonomous vehicle navigating an unsecured environment as a test case.

While permutation testing is recognized for producing valid $p$-values under permutations, precise computation of exact $p$ many times proves unfeasible due to combinatorial complexity. Addressing this limitation, we propose a novel method that leverages the internal structure of specific test statistics to determine exact permutation distributions efficiently. Our approach models the test statistic as a linear function of data within specific dimensions determined by parameter vectors, which we use to identify corresponding permutation configurations via an adaptive enumeration strategy. This framework applies broadly to numerous statistical models, including two-sample hypothesis testing, MANOVA, and robust regression. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves performance gains of several orders of magnitude compared to current methodologies, effectively managing data dimensions that exceed $10^8$.

This study introduces a comprehensive, harmonized dataset covering newbuilding prices, secondhand transactions, newbuilding orders, freight rates, and scrapping prices within the global container shipping industry, spanning from 1966 to 2019. To commemorate the half-century milestone of containerization, we extend previous research by Ito and Yamashina (2020) on integrated secondhand and freight datasets through 2019 and significantly expand the dataset's breadth by incorporating newly collected information on newbuilding prices, scrap values, and orders. Using these figures, we reconstruct the historical time series for major market indices, specifically the Freight Index, Supply Index, and fundamental variables such as the price-to-newbuilding ratio and the price-to-scrap ratio. Furthermore, we analyze historical market cycles by calculating these assets' return series and evaluating their volatility, skewness, and the rate of price jumps. Our findings reveal that both the Supply Index and the price-to-newbuilding ratio functioned as effective market indicators during extensive previous cycles; however, these metrics underwent structural breaks in 1981 and again in 2004, likely triggered respectively by the introduction of the Container Index and the emergence of the global financial crisis era.

This paper extends the definition of loom areas introduced by the author's supervisor into the context of veering triangulations. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated significant potential in diverse fields, such as molecular property prediction, knowledge reasoning, and drug interaction forecasting, by learning node representations through the synthesis of external prior information and induced data patterns. CountSketch is a leading dimensionality reduction method that projects high-dimensional sparse vectors into low-dimensional space. Additionally, we explore the theoretical traits of its corresponding matrix, introducing the concept of an $\epsilon$-counting subspace codimension. Our numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of using adaptive CountSketch for finding frequent bipartite graphs and their sparse eigenvectors.

We demonstrate that collisions between two shocks localized in transverse directions within a low-energy type IIA AdS$_5$ dual gravity can be interpreted as a series expansion in gradients perpendicular to the collision plane. By precisely defining an incoming state characterized by shock rapidity and formation time, unitary evolution to the formed state allows our method to accurately predict the final state up to next-to-leading order gradients for any chosen rapidity and time scale. Our findings indicate a clear dependence on longitudinal entropy density relative to the initial entropy density, observable even at the leading order. Furthermore, the ratio of the final entropy density to its squared value serves as a suitable metric for assessing the degree of final state equilibration.

This study examines the direction-dependent resistance to dragging a solid within fluid-saturated granular material. Experiments were conducted using dyed glass beads wetted with food coloring, placed in a transparent vessel where the long-axis aligned of a cylinder (square, circular, elliptical, or rectangular cross-section) was manipulated via a tensioned string above the surface. Visual confirmation of deformation utilized either direct observation or photography enhanced with false-color contrast. Observations indicate that the supply of free fluid available for displacement around the moving object dictates the level of anisotropy exhibited by the hydrodynamic drag. Specifically, when fluid movement is restricted solely to the cylinder's ends, strong anisotropy occurs; in scenarios allowing more circumferential fluid flow, the effect is markedly diminished. These findings are interpreted through a theoretical model that mirrors experiments with dry granular systems by substituting limited fluid availability with specific internal friction characteristics. Model simulations reveal that the most intense anisotropy arises in systems with high internal friction, which corresponds to high moisture content in granular packs.

We present resolved spectral observations extending over 10 kIL in NGC 4426, heavily modified by recent intense star formation, to investigate how outflows regulate gas within their regions. Utilizing integral field spectroscopy derived from Duvet, we identify clear signatures of outflows at the galaxy's periphery characterized by elevated dispersion and [O III] emission alongside suppressed continuum and $\ion{H}\alpha$ lines relative to star-forming tracks. Comparisons with models of coherent outflows indicate limited influence at these large radii, prompting us to examine the data through a porous medium framework. Our results reveal that at the observed scale, the specific outflow momentum substantially surpasses the momentum deposited by the associated star formation activity. Furthermore, the specific outflow momentum exhibits an inverse correlation with the local star formation surface brightness, a signature consistent with the general principle that galactic outflows constrain the escape of energy and momentum resulting from exhausts.

Achieving the pinnacle of performance in computer system design and evaluation is heavily reliant on Bayesian Optimization (SO). However, applying automatic Bayesian Optimization to system configuration tasks currently faces hurdles such as the difficulty of writing code that mirrors a complex system's causal structure for optimization and the extensive manual labor required to prepare historical experiment logs. To address these challenges, we present **BoGraph**, an interactive tool that compiles an organized graphical model directly from existing system logs. By leveraging probabilistic programming, this input model facilitates the direct coding of a system's causal structure for optimization. Additionally, we describe an algorithm that enhances optimization by jointly tuning current configurations and reconfiguring historical experiment decisions. Empirical results demonstrate that using BoGraph accelerates the discovery of top-tier configurations by a factor of 2 to 5 and substantially reduces the number of evaluations needed following successful optimization.

Using a multiphase transport (AMPT) model, we examined how flow triangularity ($v_3$) manifests in $\text{Cu}+\text{Cu}$ and Au+Au collisions at the $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=200\ \text{GeV}$ energy level run by RHIC. Our analysis indicates that $v_3$ at final state is predominantly dictated by the initial spatial triangularity; in contrast, its conversion into the final state is sensitive to the specific equation of state (EOS). In the scenario where a phase transition occurs and critical phenomena are incorporated (via the mixed phase and critical critical van der Waals equations of state), the final $v_3$ in Cu+Cu collisions increases, a trend that aligns with experimental data. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the initial local $v_3$ in the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) may offer valuable insights into EOS properties, potentially aiding in the identification of a QGP phase transition and critical point.

Assessing datasets is essential for both identifying reliable sources of information and as a scaler component of machine learning workflows. However, evaluating freely available and often unsupervised formats, such as Resource Description Framework (RDF), presents unique challenges. To overcome these issues, the authors have created QaRDFEval, a new framework designed to assess RDF datasets. Utilizing a comprehensive set of quality measures, QaRDFEeval computes various semantic and structural metrics across multiple layers of the RDF model. Furthermore, it generates visual representations to facilitate the interpretation of these evaluations. Empirical testing on eleven well-known datasets confirms the practicality and effectiveness of QaRDFEval.
